newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: War's end bittersweet for Guatemala rebels.
newsitem.headline: War's end bittersweet for Guatemala rebels.

text.p: A group of left-wing Guatemalan guerrillas marched out of hiding into a disarmament camp, chanting their slogans in a bittersweet end to 36 years of civil war, and of a way of life.

"I felt sad this morning even though this is the day we've been waiting for. But I got excited when I saw the attitude and the acceptance of the people," said 2nd Lt. Amanda of the Cesar Sandino guerrilla front as she reached the camp on Saturday.

She is among 3,000 rebels of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Front (URNG) laying down arms in eight separate camps under an historic peace treaty signed in December, ending a civil war which claimed 140,000 lives, mostly poor Indians.
After disarmament the URNG will convert itself into a political party.

The URNG never won huge support among Guatemala's Mayan Indian majority but the Mayans of the town of San Jose Sinache near the guerrilla's last tent camp gave the 130 guerrillas a warm send off as they left for the disarmament camp.

More than a hundred San Jose women, in traditional purple skirts and plastic sandals, marched 16 miles (25 km) with the guerrillas to their barracks at Tululche camp where a total of 600 ex-combatants will live until disarmament ends on May 3.
The Sandino Front, named after the Nicaraguan peasant who inspired the name of that country's guerrillas, operated in the Quiche department in the steep mountains at the centre of Guatemala.
The Tululche camp in Quiche is perched on a windswept ridge a four-hour drive from the capital, and an hour from the famous Mayan market and tourist destination of Chichicastenango.
The guerrillas, dressed in olive green and accompanied by three United Nations vans, marched past small farming settlements, cornfields, pine forests and gawking villagers.
They brought less than 130 weapons -- everything from World War Two-vintage carbines to AK-47 submachine guns -- to the camp to turn in before the May 3 deadline.
Under the peace accords guerrillas must reveal the locations of arms caches and turn in machineguns and heavy artillery.
